findings.passage: In 2019 the actor Elliot Page had criticized his church as anti-LGBTQ. In 2022 Pratt said he had never been to Hillsong, the church he had been linked to, and attends Zoe Church, though not exclusively.
findings.problem: On the article's most sensitive allegation, a cold reader cannot follow who said what, when. The paragraph runs 2022 (Men's Health) -> 2022 (Daily Beast headline) -> 2019 (Page) -> 2022 (Hillsong denial) -> 2017 (photo, film) -> 'at the time'. 'His church' never says which church Page meant, though the next sentence names two. The Daily Beast headline lands before the reader knows what 'lying' refers to: the 'not a religious person' line or the Hillsong denial. 'At the time' has no anchor. And Pratt's direct 2019 reply to the anti-LGBTQ charge, which Men's Health quotes ('Nothing could be further from the truth. I am a man who believes that everyone is entitled to love who they want free from the judgment of their fellow man.', src-mh-2022 excerpt), is missing. So the only response a reader sees is 'I'm gonna, like, throw a church under the bus?', which read cold can sound like he declined to dispute the charge. The paragraph also never says what the episode shows about him, so it reads as a detour from the faith argument.
findings.acceptance_test: From this paragraph alone, a reader with no prior knowledge can say in order: what Page criticized in 2019 and which church was meant; what Pratt said in reply in 2019, in his own sourced words; what he said in 2022 about Hillsong, Zoe and being 'not a religious person'; what the Daily Beast said he misstated and on what basis; and what 'at the time' refers to. Every charge stays attributed with Pratt's response next to it, dates run in order or are explicit, and one sentence ties the episode to the portrait (for example, to his account shifting with the setting). Otherwise the paragraph is cut to what the portrait needs, keeping attribution and his response.

findings.passage: At about 19, freshly failed and, by his account, depressed, he had a job he was good at and gave the hours away.
findings.problem: The ages run backward for a reader building a timeline. The Denver office, which came first, is dated with 'I wasn't even 21.' After the collapse, the trip home and the partying, Maui comes 'at about 19,' and the limits paragraph repeats 'about 19.' The evidence record itself says 19 to 20. A cold reader either suspects an error or loses the sequence (office, collapse, home, Maui) that the 3-vs-7 test depends on.
findings.acceptance_test: The body gives one consistent age or range for the Maui stretch (for example '19 or 20') wherever it is mentioned, and a reader can order office -> collapse -> home -> Maui without the ages contradicting each other.

findings.passage: Third, what he wants from a role. A Three wants top billing. Asked about Andy in 2026, Pratt said what he loved was "being a jazz soloist, but not the lead singer."
findings.problem: Four sections earlier, the orientation paragraph told the reader he 'became a leading man' in 2014-2015. The article also reports that he 'had always wanted to play an action hero' and names his recent leads (James Reese, Mercy). A cold reader's first objection is that he has taken top billing for more than a decade. The third tip never confronts that, and the limits paragraph leaves out a limit the evidence record lists: the line came while he was discussing a return to comedy with Mike Schur. As written, the weakest of the three tips reads as the cleanest.
findings.acceptance_test: The third point or the limits paragraph acknowledges his leading-man career since 2014 and the setting of the remark, then says why the preference still discriminates or presents it as supporting rather than deciding evidence. A reader who remembers 'became a leading man' is not left with an unanswered contradiction.

findings.passage: What I liked about Andy Dwyer was it was like being a jazz soloist, but not the lead singer. Like when it was my four measures, I can go and do my little comedy thing. It can be different every time.
findings.problem: The ending's payoff quote has already been used, in 'Why not Type 3?', as the third tip. By the closing section the reader has seen the jazz-soloist line, so the final block quote reads as a repeat and the ending loses its lift.
findings.acceptance_test: The jazz-soloist wording appears in full once, ideally in the ending. Any earlier reference is a short pointer or a different piece of evidence, so the closing quote reads as new to a first-time reader.

findings.passage: Describing the years before his 2018 MTV speech, he said on _Not Dead Yet_:
findings.problem: The Three case divides his career at 'his 2018 MTV speech,' but the reader learns what that speech was (a Generation Award speech that said 'God is real') three sections later. A cold reader meets an unexplained hinge at the point where the strongest rival is being argued.
findings.acceptance_test: At first mention, a short clause tells the reader what the 2018 MTV speech was. Otherwise the Three section is worded so it does not depend on knowledge the article supplies only later.

findings.passage: broke through as Andy Dwyer on _Parks and Recreation_ (2009 to 2015), and became a leading man as Star-Lord in _Guardians of the Galaxy_ (2014) and Owen Grady in _Jurassic World_ (2015).
findings.problem: Andy carries the article: a section title, the 'clown' origin, the heavy years, the jazz-soloist tip and the ending. Yet the reader is never told what kind of character Andy is beyond Pratt's pitch of a 'super-confident dumb fat guy.' The career summary also stops in 2015, so 'a run of serious roles,' The Terminal List and Mercy arrive with no bridge across the decade in between.
findings.acceptance_test: A reader who has never seen Parks and Recreation gets a sourced one-clause sketch of Andy before the Andy sections. One dated sentence (no current-status claims) bridges his 2015-2026 career, so the comedy-return section lands with context.

findings.passage: That is the Seven's trap, described from the inside. Hope lives in the next ticket, and once the tickets are easy to get, the hole is still there.
findings.problem: By this point 'ticket' has meant his mother's plane ticket home and a friend's one-way ticket to Maui. The quote 'just get that ticket, baby' is cut before the words that show what he meant (the evidence records 'I get that ticket, I'm free sailing'), so a cold reader can't tell whether the ticket is a lottery ticket, a big break or travel. The interpretation sentence depends on that meaning.
findings.acceptance_test: A reader can tell what 'ticket' means in his remark, from a brief gloss or the fuller quote where the transcriptions agree. The interpretation either uses the echo with the Maui ticket on purpose or avoids the collision.

findings.passage: Henry said "Jesus told me to talk to you" and took him to church.
findings.problem: The Henry anecdote stops at the church door and never pays off. The faith section says he knelt at altars 'at 19' but never connects that to Henry, so a cold reader can't tell whether Henry was a conversion, one of the broken promises, or a passing episode. Placed between 'what he did there' and Rae Dawn Chong, it also breaks the shifts-to-discovery link, and its later use (against Type 6) isn't signaled.
findings.acceptance_test: Either one sourced sentence says what came of the Henry night, or the faith section ties to it as far as the record allows (without implying a link the sources don't make). A reader can say why the anecdote is in the article.

protected_passages.passage: Both accounts are his. Side by side, they show a move that runs through his life: he meets a bad stretch by finding the fun in it, first while living it and again when he tells the story.
protected_passages.reason: Turns two sourced quotes into the article's thesis without jargon. A cold reader gets the contradiction and the reason to keep reading in two sentences.

protected_passages.passage: No camera was on him. If the hidden failure had been about his worth, this was the moment to start repairing it, and he spent it on a beach.
protected_passages.reason: The clearest plain-language version of the 3-vs-7 test. Concrete, memorable, and anyone without Enneagram knowledge can follow it.

protected_passages.passage: Press tours tune a story to the room. What stays the same in every version is what he did there.
protected_passages.reason: Teaches the reader how to weigh self-report against behavior. It builds trust in the method instead of asserting certainty.

protected_passages.passage: A reader can still argue Three. The argument here is that Three explains the selling, and Seven explains the choices.
protected_passages.reason: An honest, quotable summary of the type argument that leaves the reader room to disagree. It is the most useful sentence for someone deciding between the two readings.

protected_passages.passage: Eleven years later he wants the fun back, and he has said what made it easy. The funny guy didn't have to be hurt.
protected_passages.reason: A resonant ending that ties the 2015 'image' admission, the childhood 'clown' and Schur's main-character idea into one plain line. It rewards the opening's curiosity.

assessment: Cold read: the draft orients well and earns its stakes. The 2014 'charming time' quote set against the 2017 'not in a great place' line gives a reader a sourced contradiction worth following. The type answer explains 'head triad' and 'fear' in plain steps before relying on them. The sales-to-Maui stretch is the strongest part: a reader with no Enneagram background can see the 3-vs-7 test and why the given-away shifts matter. The childhood, heavy-years and wandering-mind sections each add new evidence (the sock, the catalog cards, the Farley comparison) rather than restating the thesis, and the stated limits (self-report, auto-captions, age at Maui) build trust. The weak spots are clarity and orientation, not the core argument. The Hillsong paragraph is hard to follow on a sensitive allegation and leaves out Pratt's 2019 reply (major). Ages and several references (the 2018 MTV speech, Andy, 'ticket') assume knowledge the reader lacks. The ending's best quote is spent earlier, and the 'not the lead singer' tip doesn't face the decade of leading roles the orientation paragraph announced. Smaller notes, not filed: the body says the heavy years 'ended' with Moneyball (2011), while the FAQ puts his peak at 295 pounds in 2013; 'lasted one clause' appears twice; wing notation (7w6, 7w8) is never glossed; and the 8/6/9 section slows momentum between the hand-off to faith and the faith section. Similarity advisory: most tripped pairs match this page's own earlier Chris Pratt version, which is a self-match, not cross-subject reuse. The Florence Pugh match is a stock head-triad gloss and the Dominic Fike match is the stock phrase 'gets a full hearing below.' Neither is a reused argument, so neither is a finding. Risks: sensitive allegations (the anti-LGBTQ church criticism, the Daily Beast's 'lying' charge), contested typing, and a major thesis change from the published Type 3 all apply, so the expanded six-role jury is required.
